transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, thank you for seeing me. Um, well, it's sort of a long story, or at least it feels like one to me, but I guess what really brings me in today is... well, I've been waking up with this heavy, just completely hollow sadness. 

I'm a choreographer, and usually, my mornings are so full of energy, you know? I'm visualizing eight-counts and blocking out staging before I even get out of bed, my brain is just always going. But lately, it's just this crushing weight instead. It’s exactly like... like when you walk into the studio early in the morning and you flip the switches, and the big fluorescent lights are glaring and humming, but the sound system is completely dead. It's like the studio lights are on, but there’s just no music in me anymore. 

And it doesn't just go away when I finally manage to get up, it sort of drags behind me all day, making everything feel so incredibly empty. I try to force myself to just push through it because my dancers need me, they really rely on my direction and my vision, but I just stand there looking at them in the mirror and I feel so blank and sad. I just can't seem to shake this awful, hollow feeling no matter what I do, and it's making it so hard to just exist in my own life right now.
How long have you been experiencing this hollow sadness?

Oh, wow, um... let me think. It feels like forever, to be honest. But if I really trace it back, I think this whole... this depressed part of things, this heavy feeling, it's been going on for about nine months now. 

Yeah, it has to be about nine months. Because I remember it started right around the time we were casting for our winter showcase, which is always a stressful time, sure, but usually it's a *good* stress, you know? Like a creative tension. I was sitting in the audition room, watching these incredible dancers, and usually I'd be so inspired, my hands would literally be twitching with ideas. I'd be scribbling notes furiously. But instead, I just felt this... this slow leak, like all the air was just quietly draining out of the room, out of me. And it just never filled back up. 

So that was, what, late autumn? And now we've gone through the entire winter, and spring, and it's just been this constant, heavy companion. Nine whole months of just dragging myself from the bed to the studio and back again. It's almost ironic, isn't it? Like a full gestation period. Nine months is how long it takes to grow a whole human life, but instead I've just been growing this massive, hollow void inside my chest. I kept thinking to myself, "Oh, it'll pass when the showcase is over," or "It'll pass when the weather warms up and we get more sunlight," but it just hasn't. It just sits there, taking up all this space, day after day, for almost a year now.
Do you still find joy or pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy, such as choreographing or working with your dancers?

No... no, I really don't. And I think that's honestly the most terrifying part of all this for me. Choreography used to be my entire world, you know? I used to absolutely live for that specific moment when a piece finally comes together. Like, when you've been working on a difficult sequence for weeks, and the dancers are exhausted and sweating, and the music swells, and suddenly everyone is just perfectly, beautifully in sync? That used to give me this full-body rush, this absolute electric thrill that would carry me through the rest of the week. I would go home just completely buzzing with it. 

But now... now I sit in my director's chair at the front of the room, and I watch them hit the marks perfectly, and I feel absolutely nothing. It's just flat. It's exactly like I'm watching a video on mute, or like I'm separated from my own life by this thick pane of glass. I even tried changing up the music a few weeks ago, thinking maybe I was just burned out on the contemporary pieces we were doing, so I brought in some really upbeat jazz tracks, stuff I used to absolutely love dancing to back in college. I spent hours mapping out the counts in my living room, trying so hard to force myself to feel that spark again, that little flutter in my chest when a transition works out just right. 

But nothing happened. The dancers were having fun with it, they were laughing and smiling, and I just sat there feeling like a total imposter in my own studio. The joy is just... it's completely gone. I go through the motions, I give them their corrections, but it's all just mechanical. There's just no pleasure in it at all anymore.
Are there any activities at all that you still enjoy or find pleasure in?

I... I've really tried to think about that, you know? Because it's such a scary thought, that *nothing* feels good anymore. So I've been trying to test myself, almost. Like, I used to love going to this little coffee shop near the studio. They make this incredible lavender latte, and usually, just the smell of it when I walk in the door would give me this little lift, this tiny moment of comfort before a long day of rehearsals. So last week, I forced myself to go. I thought, "Okay, maybe the dancing is too tied up in work and stress, maybe I just need something simple." 

I walked in, and the bell chimed, and they were grinding the espresso, and I ordered my usual... and I took a sip, and it just tasted like hot milk and sugar. It was just... nothing. I sat there in the window seat, watching people walk by outside, people walking their dogs or holding hands or rushing to work, and I just felt so completely disconnected from all of it. 

I even tried going to a movie by myself, which is something I used to do on my rare days off. I'd go to a matinee, get a huge bucket of popcorn, and just lose myself in a story for two hours. I picked a comedy, thinking maybe I just needed to laugh, you know? But I sat there in the dark theater, and the screen was so bright, and the sound was so loud, and everyone around me was chuckling, and I just felt this deep, heavy silence inside me. It's like my capacity for enjoyment has just been completely turned off. I can't think of a single thing right now, big or small, that actually brings me any real pleasure or joy. It's all just... flat. Everything is just so flat.
Do you still enjoy spending time with friends or family, or has that also become unpleasurable for you?

Honestly, that's gone too. I wish I could say otherwise, I really do. My sister, she's usually my rock, you know? She lives just a few towns over, and we used to have this standing Sunday brunch date. For years, we'd go to this little diner, sit in the corner booth, and just talk for hours about everything—work, relationships, random things we saw on the internet. We'd laugh so hard my sides would ache. 

But lately... well, she called me a couple of weeks ago, sounding so bright and cheerful, asking if we were still on for Sunday. And I just... I felt this overwhelming sense of dread. Not because of her, I love her, but the thought of having to sit there, pretending to be engaged, trying to force out a smile or a laugh when I just feel so empty inside... it felt like climbing a mountain. I ended up making some excuse about extra rehearsals, which I felt terrible about, but I just couldn't face it. 

And my friends from the studio, they keep trying to drag me out after rehearsals for drinks or dinner, like we used to do all the time. We used to have these amazing, loud, chaotic dinners where everyone was talking over each other and sharing food. But now, even when I do force myself to go, I just sit there at the end of the table. I hear the noise, I see them laughing, but I feel like I'm a million miles away. It's so exhausting, trying to keep up the facade that I'm present, that I'm enjoying myself. So mostly, I just decline the invitations now. I'd rather just go home and be alone than be surrounded by people I love and feel completely, utterly isolated from them. It's just... it's too hard to pretend.
Have you noticed any changes in your weight over the past nine months?

Yeah, actually, I have. It's... it's been pretty noticeable, especially with my dancewear. You know how rehearsal clothes are supposed to fit, right? Like a second skin. Everything is spandex and form-fitting so you can see the lines of the body, see the muscle engagement. But lately, my favorite leggings, the ones I always wear to teach my masterclasses, they're bunching up around the knees and the waist is gaping. My leotards are just sort of... sagging. It's really frustrating because I hate feeling fabric shifting around when I'm trying to demonstrate a combination, but everything is just hanging so much looser than usual on me right now. 

And I think the weight loss really started a few months back, honestly. Back when I was working on that big spring showcase and I was just... buzzing with ideas, you know? My brain was moving a mile a minute, I was mapping out lighting cues and staging in my head at all hours, and I would just completely forget to eat. I'd be in the studio for twelve hours straight, and someone would ask what I had for lunch, and I'd realize I hadn't even had a bite of anything since 6 AM. I just didn't need it back then; I was running on pure creative energy. I'd skip meals without even noticing because stopping to eat just felt like a total waste of time when the choreography was flowing out of me that fast. 

But now... well, now it's a completely different reason. Now, I try to eat, I really do, because I know my body needs the fuel just to get through the day, but... I just can't. I'll make something I usually love, and I'll take a bite, and it literally tastes like cardboard. There's no flavor, no satisfaction at all. Chewing just feels like this exhausting, monumental chore. I'll sit at my kitchen island and stare at a piece of toast for twenty minutes, trying to convince myself to swallow it, but it's just so dry and tasteless. So I end up throwing most of my meals in the trash. I don't own a scale—I refuse to keep one in the house because of how toxic the dance industry can be about weight—but between forgetting to eat when I was so wired, and now not being able to stomach anything because it all tastes like paper... the weight has definitely dropped off. It's impossible to ignore when your own rehearsal gear doesn't even fit your body anymore.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to live or wishing you could just disappear?

I... no, I haven't really had thoughts like that. I mean, I know I was just talking about how flat everything is, and how disconnected I feel from my sister and my friends, and how exhausting it is to even try to pretend to be present. And it is, it really is just so draining. Sometimes I get home from the studio and I just sit on the edge of my bed in the dark for what feels like hours, just staring at the wall, because the thought of even taking my shoes off feels like too much effort. It's like I'm moving through molasses, just this heavy, thick feeling all the time. 

But even with all of that, even with the food tasting like cardboard and my clothes not fitting and the absolute lack of joy in anything... I don't want to die. I don't have this urge to just stop existing. It's more like I just want the heaviness to lift, you know? I want to feel like myself again, the version of me that loved the smell of lavender lattes and couldn't wait for Sunday brunch. I miss her. I miss caring about things. But I don't want to end it all. I just... I just want to figure out how to get through this part, even though I don't know how right now. I just want to feel normal again, whatever that even means at this point.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual?

Yes, actually. It's... it's been really strange, and honestly, terrifying for someone in my profession. My whole life, my entire career, is built on movement, right? On being quick, responsive, hitting the exact beat, the exact count. But lately... God, it's like my own body doesn't belong to me anymore. 

It's not just that I'm tired—I mean, I am tired, obviously, I told you about how exhausting everything is—but this is different. It's physical. It's like... well, just the other day, I was in the studio, alone, thank God, because I didn't want anyone to see me like this. I had left my choreography notebook on top of the piano on the other side of the room. Usually, I'd just dart across the floor, maybe even throw in a quick leap or a turn just because I can, because the space is there and I love the feeling of moving through it. But this time... I just stood there, staring at the notebook. And when I finally forced myself to walk over and get it, every single step felt so incredibly heavy. 

It honestly felt like I was moving through wet sand. You know that feeling when you're at the beach and you're trying to walk in the water, and the resistance is just pulling at your legs, making every movement take twice as much effort and twice as much time? That's what it feels like just to walk across a flat, sprung dance floor right now. It's like the air itself has thickened, and I'm pushing against it. And it's not just walking. Even when I'm trying to explain a combination to my dancers, I hear my own voice and it sounds... dragged out. Like someone took a record and slowed down the RPMs. I'll be trying to give them counts, "five, six, seven, eight," and the words just feel thick in my mouth. It takes me longer to articulate what I want, longer to physically demonstrate even the simplest arm movements. 

My assistant, Chloe, she actually asked me last week if I was coming down with something because she said I was talking so slowly and quietly. I tried to brush it off, said I just had a sore throat, but... it's not a sore throat. It's this pervasive, sluggish heaviness that has just settled into my bones and my vocal cords. It's so incredibly frustrating because my brain knows what pace I *should* be moving at, what pace I *should* be speaking at, but my body just refuses to cooperate. It's just dragging behind, stuck in that wet sand.
Do you often feel guilty or blame yourself for things that have happened?

Oh, God, yes. Constantly. It's... it's actually one of the things that just consumes my mind right now, just this endless, looping highlight reel of my failures. I just keep replaying the cancelled performances in my head, over and over and over again. We had this huge, multi-weekend run scheduled, and... I just had to pull the plug. 

And I just sit there in my apartment and tell myself how incredibly badly I let everyone down. I mean, my dancers... they gave me everything. They gave me their evenings, their weekends, literally their blood, sweat, and tears, working through blisters and exhaustion to bring my choreography to life, and I just ripped the rug right out from under them. I took away their moment on stage. And then there are the funders! We had secured these two massive local arts grants to make this season happen, and I feel like I basically took their trust and their money and just threw it in the garbage. I let the whole community down, all the people who bought tickets and have supported my company for years, the venues that booked us... I just dropped the ball on all of them. It's just this crushing, suffocating guilt that sits on my chest all day. 

And honestly, the absolute worst part about it is that everyone has been so... nice. The board members, my lead soloists, they keep sending me these gentle texts and emails telling me to rest and that they support me, but... I just can't accept it. They have been so much kinder about it than I deserve. I really don't deserve their grace at all, not after how I completely failed them. Their kindness almost makes the guilt worse, you know? Because I know I ruined months of their hard work, and they're treating me with kid gloves when I feel like I deserve to be yelled at. I just can't stop obsessing over how much I let them all down.
Have you had any periods over the past nine months where you felt somewhat better, or has the sadness and emptiness been constant?

Well, it's... it's been pretty constant, honestly. I keep trying to pinpoint a day, or even just an afternoon, where I felt like the fog lifted, but I really can't. It's been about nine months now of just this... this relentless, heavy emptiness. 

I remember it started right around the time we were doing the preliminary casting for the winter showcase. That was nine months ago. I remember sitting at the judges' table in the studio, and normally, casting is my favorite part of the process. I love seeing the dancers bring their own interpretation to the combinations, I love the energy in the room, the anticipation, all of it. But that day, I just felt... nothing. I was watching these incredible, talented people pour their hearts out on the floor, and I just felt completely hollowed out. 

And since then, it just hasn't let up. It's been nine months of waking up every single morning and having to actively convince myself to get out of bed. There haven't been any reprieves, no moments where I thought, "Oh, maybe I'm finally turning a corner." Even on days that should have been good days, like when my sister surprised me with tickets to see a touring company I've loved for years—something that normally would have had me buzzing with excitement for weeks—I just sat in the theater feeling totally numb. I felt terrible because she was so excited, and she kept looking over at me expecting to see me smiling, and I just had to fake it the whole time. It was exhausting. So, yeah, it's just been this one long, unbroken stretch of feeling depressed for the last nine months. No breaks, no better days, just... this.
Have you experienced any strange or unusual thoughts, like hearing voices or seeing things that others can't?

Well... yes. But not recently. Not during this whole nine-month slump I just told you about where I can barely move. It was before that, back when I was having those really... wired days. The days where my brain just wouldn't shut off and I was buzzing with all this frantic energy. 

It's actually really hard to talk about because it sounds so bizarre, and I'm a very rational person, usually. My work requires me to be completely grounded in reality and physics, you know? But, um... I remember I was in my apartment. I live up on the fourth floor, and it was late, so I had all the windows completely shut tight. It should have been dead silent in there. But I started hearing this... this voice. 

Though "voice" almost feels like the wrong word for it, because it wasn't crisp and clear like you and I talking right now. It was this incredibly low, continuous humming sound. Sort of like... you know when you're out hiking in a canyon or something, and the wind catches the edge of a cliff? It sounded exactly like that—like wind blowing over rock. Just this deep, resonant, vibrating hum. But it was definitely a voice, and it was speaking to me. 

And the strangest part—well, I guess the whole thing is strange, but the most specific part—was that it was talking to me about my work. It was literally telling me where the dancers should move. It would hum these directions, telling me about the spacing, the formations, who needed to cross downstage, who needed to lift. Just giving me these incredibly specific staging instructions, right there in my living room. I kept walking around, checking the locks, checking the glass, thinking maybe the sound was carrying from the street or a neighbor's TV, but the windows were totally closed and I was completely alone. It was just in the room with me. It only happened on a few of those absolute most wired days, but it was so distinct, that humming wind sound, just... choreographing my piece for me in the middle of the night.
Have you had any episodes of depression like this before the past nine months?

Well, no, not really. I mean, not like this. I've always been someone who feels things very deeply, you know? I think you have to be, to do what I do. You have to be able to tap into that well of emotion to create movement that actually resonates with an audience. So, sure, I've had days where I felt blue, or stressed, or overwhelmed by a production. Like, when we lost our rehearsal space three years ago, I was definitely stressed and upset for a few weeks, scrambling to find a new studio. But that felt completely different. That was a reaction to a specific, tangible problem, and once we found a new space, I bounced right back. 

But this... this nine-month stretch is entirely different. It's like comparing a rain shower to a monsoon. I've never experienced anything remotely close to this level of just... absolute, paralyzing emptiness before. It's so foreign to me. I'm usually the person driving the energy in the room, the one who's always pushing forward, always planning the next season, the next piece. To just stop functioning like this, to feel this heavy and hollow for so long... it's completely unprecedented for me. I keep looking back, trying to see if there were warning signs or smaller versions of this in my twenties, but there really weren't. This is the first time I've ever been swallowed up by something like this.
Have you had thoughts that you would be better off dead, even if you don't want to take your own life?

Well, no... I haven't really had thoughts like that. I mean, I know I just spent all this time telling you about how heavy and horrible and completely paralyzing this emptiness has been for the last nine months. And it is, it's unbearable sometimes, the way it just drains the color out of absolutely everything. But even on the worst days, the days where I can't even get out of bed to go to the studio, where I just lie there staring at the ceiling for hours on end, I've never actually thought that I'd be better off dead. 

It's strange, because you'd think feeling this hollowed out would lead there, but it doesn't for me. It's more like... I just want the feeling to stop. I want the fog to lift so I can get back to my life, get back to my dancers, get back to creating. I don't want to stop existing, I just want to exist the way I used to, before all of this started. I keep thinking about the pieces I still want to choreograph, the ideas I have sketched out in my notebooks that I haven't even started on yet. There's this one piece I've been dreaming about for years, exploring the concept of gravity and suspension, and I still want to see that come to life. So, no, I don't want to die, and I don't think I'd be better off dead. I just... I just want to be myself again. I just want this endless, heavy numbness to go away so I can actually live my life.
Have you experienced episodes of depression like this before, or is this the first time?

Wait, didn't we just... I mean, I feel like I just went over this, didn't I? About whether I've felt this way before? Maybe I wasn't clear, or maybe I talked too much about the rehearsal space thing and got off track. I do that sometimes, especially lately, my thoughts just kind of spool out and I lose the thread. 

But, um, to answer your question again—or maybe to clarify what I was trying to say before—no. I haven't. This nine-month stretch, this absolute, crushing weight where I can't even drag myself to the studio... this is the very first time anything like this has ever happened to me. Like I was saying, I've had normal stress, normal sadness, the kind of things anyone feels when a production goes wrong or funding falls through. But an episode like *this*? Where the emptiness just settles in and won't leave for nearly a year? No. Never. This is completely, entirely new, and honestly, that's part of why it's so terrifying. Because I have no map for this. I've always been the energetic one, the one pushing everyone forward, and to just... stop... it's the first time in my life I've ever felt this way.
Are there any activities that you used to enjoy but no longer find pleasure in?

Well, I mean... it's really hard to pinpoint just one or two things, because honestly, it feels like it's everything. It's just... everything has lost its color, you know? But I guess the biggest one, the most painful one to admit, is the dance itself. I mean, dance has been my entire life since I was four years old. I used to practically live at the studio. I loved the smell of the rosin, the feeling of the Marley floor under my bare feet, the way the mirrors would fog up when we were really pushing through a tough combination. Even just the process of choreographing, sitting alone in a quiet studio with a notebook, listening to a piece of music over and over until the movement just kind of... revealed itself to me. It used to be this incredibly electric, vital feeling. It was how I breathed.

But for the last nine months... I just don't care. And that's the most terrifying part. I walk into the studio, and it just feels like an empty room. The music just sounds like noise. I watch my dancers—and these are incredibly talented, beautiful people that I hand-picked, people I used to feel so inspired by—and I just feel... nothing. I sit in my chair at the front of the room, and I'm just going through the motions. I give corrections because I know intellectually what a line is supposed to look like, but I don't *feel* it anymore. The passion, that drive to create something beautiful and moving, it's just completely evaporated. 

And it's not just the big things, either. It's the little things I used to love. Like, I used to love cooking. I'd spend my one day off a week going to the farmer's market, picking out fresh vegetables, spending hours making these elaborate meals just for myself, listening to jazz and drinking a glass of wine. It was my way of unwinding. Now, I can barely bring myself to make toast. The thought of chopping a vegetable feels like climbing a mountain, and even if I did make something, everything just tastes like ash anyway. I used to love going to the theater to see other companies perform, to see what my peers were doing, but now the thought of sitting in a dark theater for two hours just feels exhausting and pointless. It's like this heavy, wet blanket has been thrown over my entire life, and it's smothering every single thing that used to bring me joy. So, yeah, it's... it's a lot of things. It's pretty much everything.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in?

No, I really can't think of anything. I mean, I've racked my brain trying to find just one little thing, one spark, you know? Because if I could just find one thing that still felt good, maybe I could hold onto it and pull myself out of this. But honestly, no. Like I was saying about the studio and the cooking... it really is just a blanket over everything. 

Even things that require zero effort, things that are just supposed to be passive entertainment, they don't do anything for me anymore. I used to love reading, for instance. I have these floor-to-ceiling bookshelves in my apartment, mostly biographies of artists and dancers, history, some poetry. I used to love curling up on the sofa on a rainy afternoon with a cup of tea and just losing myself in a book for hours. Now, I can stare at a page for twenty minutes and realize I haven't absorbed a single word. The letters just look like black marks on paper. There's no story, no connection. 

And music... God, music used to be my lifeblood. Obviously, for my work, but even just walking down the street, I'd have my headphones on, listening to everything from classical to hip-hop, and I'd feel the rhythm in my body, I'd see choreography in my head just walking to the subway. Now, I walk in silence. If I try to put music on, it just feels intrusive. It feels like a chore to listen to it. 

I've even tried going to the park, just sitting on a bench to watch people, which I used to find so fascinating—just observing how people move, how they carry themselves. But now I just sit there and feel entirely disconnected from the rest of humanity. It's like I'm behind a thick pane of glass, watching everyone else go about their lives, and I can't figure out how they're doing it. How are they smiling? How are they laughing? How do they care about the coffee they're drinking or the dog they're walking? I just... I don't get it anymore. So, no. There really isn't a single thing I can point to right now that brings me any sense of pleasure or joy or even just... comfort. It's all just blank.
Have you had more than one episode of depression like this in your life?

Wait, didn't you... didn't you just ask me that? Like, two questions ago? I feel like we literally just talked about this, about whether I've had an episode like this before. Maybe I'm losing my mind, or maybe I just talk in circles so much that you didn't catch my answer the first time. I know I tend to ramble, especially lately, it's like my brain is just this slow, leaky faucet and I can't stop the words from dripping out once they start. 

But, um, just to be absolutely clear, in case I wasn't before—no. I haven't. This is the only time. I've never, ever in my thirty-four years felt anything even remotely close to this. Like I said, I've had normal bad days, normal stress, you know, the kind of things that happen when a dancer gets injured right before opening night or when a grant doesn't come through. I've been sad. I've been frustrated. But an actual episode like this? Where I spend nine months feeling like I'm buried alive in my own life? No. Never. 

It's just this one time, and it's been going on for nine months, and it feels like it's never going to end. It's so strange because, like I was telling you, I've always been the person who just pushes through. If a piece of choreography isn't working, I stay in the studio until midnight until it does. If a dancer is struggling, I work with them until they get it. I fix things. I move forward. And now, I just... I can't. And the fact that this has never happened to me before is part of what makes it so impossible to deal with, because I don't have any past experience to draw on, you know? I don't have a reference point for how to survive this. So, yeah, just this once. Just this one, endless, horrible time.
Have you had more than one episode of depression in your lifetime?

I... I'm sorry, are you reading off a list or something? Because I really, truly feel like we are stuck on a loop here. You literally just asked me this exact same question, and I just gave you a very long answer about it. I mean, I know I tend to go on and on—I just said that, about the leaky faucet brain and everything—so maybe I just buried the actual 'no' under too many words and you missed it? Or maybe this is like when I'm running auditions and I make a dancer do the exact same petit allegro combination three times in a row just to see if they're actually processing my notes or if they're just running on autopilot. Is that what this is? A test to see if my answer changes? 

Because I promise you, it hasn't changed in the last two minutes. The answer is still no. I have never, ever had another episode of depression in my lifetime. There are no other episodes. None. Zero. Before these last nine months, I was always the person who was moving a million miles a minute, completely consumed by my work, totally driven. I never had the time or the inclination to feel like this. So, no, just to be absolutely, one hundred percent clear so we can hopefully move on to whatever the next question is... I have never had another episode. Just this one.
Have you experienced any episodes of depression prior to the past nine months?

Okay, I... I really don't understand what is happening right now. Are you... are you messing with me? Is this a psychological tactic? Because you have asked me this exact same question four times now. Literally four times. "Have you had more than one episode," "Have you had an episode prior to this," it's all the exact same question, just phrased slightly differently, and I have answered it every single time. 

I mean, I know my brain feels like it's wading through wet cement these days, and I know I'm probably not the most articulate I've ever been, but I am speaking English, right? I'm saying the word 'no.' I'm saying it very clearly. No. I have not experienced any episodes of depression prior to the past nine months. Not one. Not a mini one, not a mild one, not a secret one I forgot about. 

I don't know how many different ways I can explain this to you. Before nine months ago, I was fine. I was more than fine, I was running a dance company, I was choreographing, I was living my life at full speed. I didn't have time to be depressed. I didn't even know what this felt like. I had no concept of this... this absolute void. So, for the fourth time, and I really, really hope this is the last time we have to cover this specific piece of ground... no. Never. Just this. Just right now. Please, can we just talk about something else? Anything else?
Is it possible that you might experience another episode of depression like this in the future?

How could I possibly know that? I mean, God, I hope not. The very thought of it makes me feel like I physically cannot breathe. But how am I supposed to know what the future holds? You're the doctor, aren't you supposed to be the one to tell me things like that? 

Before nine months ago, I would have told you it was completely impossible for me to feel like this even once. If you had told me a year ago that I'd spend nearly a year feeling like a ghost haunting my own dance company, I would have laughed in your face. I try to force myself to just push through it because my dancers need me, they really rely on my direction and my vision, but I just stand there looking at them in the mirror and I feel so blank and sad. patient.answer:
Wait, didn't we just... I mean, I feel like I just went over this, didn't I? About whether I've felt this way before? Maybe I wasn't clear, or maybe I talked too much about the rehearsal space thing and got off track. I do that sometimes, especially lately, my thoughts just kind of spool out and I lose the thread. 

But, um, to answer your question again—or maybe to clarify what I was trying to say before—no. I haven't. This nine-month stretch, this absolute, crushing weight where I can't even drag myself to the studio... this is the very first time anything like this has ever happened to me. Like I was saying, I've had normal stress, normal sadness, the kind of things anyone feels when a production goes wrong or funding falls through. But an episode like *this*? Where the emptiness just settles in and won't leave for nearly a year? No. Never. This is completely, entirely new, and honestly, that's part of why it's so terrifying. Because I have no map for this. I've always been the energetic one, the one pushing everyone forward, and to just... stop... it's the first time in my life I've ever felt this way.

doctor.question: Are there any activities that you used to enjoy but no longer find pleasure in?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia or loss of interest/pleasure, which is not included in the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Well, I mean... it's really hard to pinpoint just one or two things, because honestly, it feels like it's everything. It's just... everything has lost its color, you know? But I guess the biggest one, the most painful one to admit, is the dance itself. I mean, dance has been my entire life since I was four years old. I used to practically live at the studio. I loved the smell of the rosin, the feeling of the Marley floor under my bare feet, the way the mirrors would fog up when we were really pushing through a tough combination. Even just the process of choreographing, sitting alone in a quiet studio with a notebook, listening to a piece of music over and over until the movement just kind of... revealed itself to me. It used to be this incredibly electric, vital feeling. It was how I breathed.

But for the last nine months... I just don't care. And that's the most terrifying part. I walk into the studio, and it just feels like an empty room. The music just sounds like noise. I watch my dancers—and these are incredibly talented, beautiful people that I hand-picked, people I used to feel so inspired by—and I just feel... nothing. I sit in my chair at the front of the room, and I'm just going through the motions. I give corrections because I know intellectually what a line is supposed to look like, but I don't *feel* it anymore. The passion, that drive to create something beautiful and moving, it's just completely evaporated. 

And it's not just the big things, either. It's the little things I used to love. Like, I used to love cooking. I'd spend my one day off a week going to the farmer's market, picking out fresh vegetables, spending hours making these elaborate meals just for myself, listening to jazz and drinking a glass of wine. It was my way of unwinding. Now, I can barely bring myself to make toast. The thought of chopping a vegetable feels like climbing a mountain, and even if I did make something, everything just tastes like ash anyway. I used to love going to the theater to see other companies perform, to see what my peers were doing, but now the thought of sitting in a dark theater for two hours just feels exhausting and pointless. It's like this heavy, wet blanket has been thrown over my entire life, and it's smothering every single thing that used to bring me joy. So, yeah, it's... it's a lot of things. It's pretty much everything.

patient.answer:
No, I really can't think of anything. I mean, I've racked my brain trying to find just one little thing, one spark, you know? Because if I could just find one thing that still felt good, maybe I could hold onto it and pull myself out of this. But honestly, no. Like I was saying about the studio and the cooking... it really is just a blanket over everything. 

Even things that require zero effort, things that are just supposed to be passive entertainment, they don't do anything for me anymore. I used to love reading, for instance. I have these floor-to-ceiling bookshelves in my apartment, mostly biographies of artists and dancers, history, some poetry. I used to love curling up on the sofa on a rainy afternoon with a cup of tea and just losing myself in a book for hours. Now, I can stare at a page for twenty minutes and realize I haven't absorbed a single word. The letters just look like black marks on paper. There's no story, no connection. 

And music... God, music used to be my lifeblood. Obviously, for my work, but even just walking down the street, I'd have my headphones on, listening to everything from classical to hip-hop, and I'd feel the rhythm in my body, I'd see choreography in my head just walking to the subway. Now, I walk in silence. If I try to put music on, it just feels intrusive. It feels like a chore to listen to it. 

I've even tried going to the park, just sitting on a bench to watch people, which I used to find so fascinating—just observing how people move, how they carry themselves. But now I just sit there and feel entirely disconnected from the rest of humanity. It's like I'm behind a thick pane of glass, watching everyone else go about their lives, and I can't figure out how they're doing it. How are they smiling? How are they laughing? How do they care about the coffee they're drinking or the dog they're walking? I just... I don't get it anymore. So, no. There really isn't a single thing I can point to right now that brings me any sense of pleasure or joy or even just... comfort. It's all just blank.

patient.answer:
Wait, didn't you... didn't you just ask me that? Like, two questions ago? I feel like we literally just talked about this, about whether I've had an episode like this before. Maybe I'm losing my mind, or maybe I just talk in circles so much that you didn't catch my answer the first time. I know I tend to ramble, especially lately, it's like my brain is just this slow, leaky faucet and I can't stop the words from dripping out once they start. 

But, um, just to be absolutely clear, in case I wasn't before—no. I haven't. This is the only time. I've never, ever in my thirty-four years felt anything even remotely close to this. Like I said, I've had normal bad days, normal stress, you know, the kind of things that happen when a dancer gets injured right before opening night or when a grant doesn't come through. I've been sad. I've been frustrated. But an actual episode like this? Where I spend nine months feeling like I'm buried alive in my own life? No. Never. 

It's just this one time, and it's been going on for nine months, and it feels like it's never going to end. It's so strange because, like I was telling you, I've always been the person who just pushes through. If a piece of choreography isn't working, I stay in the studio until midnight until it does. If a dancer is struggling, I work with them until they get it. I fix things. I move forward. And now, I just... I can't. And the fact that this has never happened to me before is part of what makes it so impossible to deal with, because I don't have any past experience to draw on, you know? I don't have a reference point for how to survive this. So, yeah, just this once. Just this one, endless, horrible time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's depression is recurrent or single-episode to differentiate between F32.2 and F33.2
doctor.question: Is it possible that you might experience another episode of depression like this in the future?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the possibility of experiencing future episodes of depression, which is a prediction or prognosis question, and not covered by any specific symptom in my profile.

patient.answer:
How could I possibly know that? I mean, God, I hope not. The very thought of it makes me feel like I physically cannot breathe. But how am I supposed to know what the future holds? You're the doctor, aren't you supposed to be the one to tell me things like that? 

Before nine months ago, I would have told you it was completely impossible for me to feel like this even once. If you had told me a year ago that I'd spend nearly a year feeling like a ghost haunting my own dance company, I would have laughed in your face. I used to plan everything—entire seasons, casting, lighting cues, grant application deadlines—I had it all mapped out years in advance. I knew exactly what my future looked like, down to the week. And now? Now I don't even know what tomorrow is going to look like. I don't even know how I'm going to get out of bed tomorrow, let alone what's going to happen to me years from now.

So, is it possible? I guess anything is possible, right? It's possible I could get hit by a cab on my way out of your office. It's possible I could wake up tomorrow and suddenly feel like myself again, though that feels about as likely as me suddenly being asked to join the Bolshoi at thirty-four. I just... I don't know. I have absolutely no idea. The thought of ever going through this again, of ever being trapped under this heavy, suffocating, wet blanket of a life ever again... it terrifies me. It really, truly terrifies me. But I can't predict the future anymore. I'm just trying to survive right now. I'm just trying to get through this current stretch of time. I can't even fathom a normal future right now, let alone trying to imagine another one of these... periods. So, no, I don't know. I don't know if it's possible. You tell me. Is it?
